title: Evidentially, My Dear Tariana
bodyHtml:
Tariana is an endangered language spoken in the Vaupés River area in Brazil, close to the border with Colombia. There are about 100 speakers of Tariana today, while there are a further 1,500 Tariana people who do not speak the language.

One morning, Antônia, Cândido, Margarida, João, Maria, and Emílio were playing a detective game, in which they had to discover who had just “poisoned” their sleeping friend Ismael! They very quickly decided that he had drunk some poisoned manioc-flour, a mixture of cassava (or tapioca) flour and water. When asked what happened to Ismael, their responses were as follows:

SpeakerTariana StatementEnglish TranslationEvidence for Claim
AntôniaDiha kawhi-nuku diiɾakaHe drank manioc-flourAntônia saw Ismael drink it before he (Ismael) fell asleep.
CândidoMayẽ kawhi-nuku diiɾanihkaIsmael drank manioc-flourCândido saw some manioc-flour on Ismael’s upper lip (like a “milk mustache”).
MargaridaDiha kawhi-nuku diiɾamahkaHe drank manioc-flourMargarida had heard Ismael slurping his manioc-flour in the room next door.
JoãoMayẽ kawhi-nuku diiɾasikaIsmael drank manioc-flourJoão knew that Ismael took some of his sister’s manioc-flour every morning.
MariaDiha kawhi-nuku diiɾapidakaHe drank manioc-flourIsmael told Maria (before falling asleep) that he (Ismael) had drunk some.
EmílioMayẽ kawhi-nuku diiɾamahkaIsmael drank manioc-flourEmílio could smell manioc-flour on Ismael’s breath.

First, they suspected José, so they went to his house. They investigated the house and spoke to a key witness (José’s mom). They all concluded José was innocent—he had an alibi! When asked what José had been doing, their responses were as follows:

SpeakerTariana StatementEnglish TranslationEvidence for Claim
AntôniaJuse iɾida dimanikakaJosé was playing soccerAntônia saw José playing soccer on the field by the road.
CândidoJuse iɾida dimanikanihkaJosé was playing soccerCândido saw that both José and José’s soccer equipment were missing.
MargaridaJuse iɾida dimanikasikaJosé was playing soccerMargarida knew it was time for José’s weekly soccer match.
JoãoNaha iɾida namanikakaThey were playing soccerJoão could see José playing soccer with his brother.
MariaNaha iɾida namanikapidakaThey were playing soccerMaria was told by José’s mum that José was playing soccer with his brother.
EmílioNaha iɾida namanikanihkaThey were playing soccerEmílio saw that José’s soccer ball and both sets of soccer shoes were missing.

Next, they went to Ismael’s house. Again they looked around, and they spoke to a second key witness (Ismael’s sister, Olívia). They agreed she was acting very suspiciously, as she wouldn’t say what she was doing at the time of Ismael’s “death”. This time, they didn’t all agree. When asked what they thought had happened, their responses were as follows:

SpeakerTariana StatementEnglish TranslationEvidence for Claim
AntôniaÓli dukwasikaOlívia was sleeping in the hammockAntônia believed that Olívia always sleeps all morning.
CândidoShe was swimmingCândido saw that Olívia’s clothes were wet.
MargaridaDuha duayhamahkaShe was swimmingMargarida had heard Olívia splashing around in the river earlier.
JoãoÓli kawhi-nuku dunimahkaOlívia was making manioc-flourJoão could smell manioc-flour in the kitchen.
MariaShe was making manioc-flourMaria was told by Ismael’s dad that Olívia had been making manioc-flour.
EmílioDuha hinipuku dumeyutanihkaShe was raking the gardenEmílio saw that the garden had recently been raked.

When João and Maria shared their information, they told Olívia:

“ mayẽ piinunihka!” You killed Ismael!

They began explaining all of the things they had come across that morning. They establish that Olívia had also gone swimming, and that Leonardo had raked the garden before going to lie down in the hammock.

H3 table. For each statement below (numbered 1 through 4), three possible pieces of evidence are given (labelled A, B, and C).

SpeakerTariana StatementEnglish TranslationPossible Evidence for Claim
1)LeonardoÓli duayhakaOlívia was swimmingA. Leonardo knew that Olívia liked swimming.
B. Leonardo had seen Olívia swimming in the river.
C. Leonardo saw that Olívia’s clothes were wet.
2)MariaLeó hinipuku dimeyutasikaLeonardo was raking the gardenA. Maria knew that Leonardo raked the garden every morning.
B. Leonardo smelt of the garden.
C. Maria saw that someone had raked the garden.
3)JoãoDiha hinipuku dimeyutamahkaHe was raking the gardenA. Leonardo smelt of the garden.
B. João had heard Leonardo raking the garden.
C. João saw that someone had raked the garden.
4)EmílioLeó dikwanihkaLeonardo was sleeping in the hammockA. Leonardo told Emílio that he (Leonardo) had been asleep.
B. Emílio saw that someone had been sleeping in the hammock.
C. Leonardo looked well-rested.

H4 table. Fill in the gaps (d)-(h) with the correct Tariana translation.

SpeakerTariana StatementEnglish TranslationEvidence for Claim
CândidoYou were swimmingCândido had overheard Olívia confirm that she (Olívia) had gone swimming.
MargaridaHe was raking the gardenMargarida saw that Leonardo’s clothes had bits of grass and leaves on them.
OlíviaLeonardo was sleeping in the hammockOlívia knew that Leonardo always lies down in the hammock after gardening.
AntôniaYou drank manioc-flourAntônia saw a dirty cup next to the hammock where Leonardo had been sleeping.
OlíviaThey were playing soccerOlívia had heard a soccer game going on while she was swimming.

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the gaps (a) and (b) by giving Cândido's and Maria's statements in Tariana.
questions.promptHtml: (a) Cândido: She was swimming — Cândido saw that Olívia’s clothes were wet.
(b) Maria: She was making manioc-flour — Maria was told by Ismael’s dad that Olívia had been making manioc-flour.

questions.partPrompt: What Tariana word should replace (c) in “___(c)___ mayẽ piinunihka!” (You killed Ismael!)?
For each statement (1-4) in the H3 table, say which of the three pieces of evidence (A, B, C) the speaker may have had in mind. You may give zero, one, or more than one option.

questions.promptHtml: 2) Maria: Leó hinipuku dimeyutasika — Leonardo was raking the garden
3) João: Diha hinipuku dimeyutamahka — He was raking the garden
4) Emílio: Leó dikwanihka — Leonardo was sleeping in the hammock

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the gaps (d)-(h) in the H4 table with the correct Tariana translation.
questions.promptHtml: (d) Cândido: You were swimming — Cândido had overheard Olívia confirm that she (Olívia) had gone swimming.
(e) Margarida: He was raking the garden — Margarida saw that Leonardo’s clothes had bits of grass and leaves on them.
(f) Olívia: Leonardo was sleeping in the hammock — Olívia knew that Leonardo always lies down in the hammock after gardening.
(g) Antônia: You drank manioc-flour — Antônia saw a dirty cup next to the hammock where Leonardo had been sleeping.
(h) Olívia: They were playing soccer — Olívia had heard a soccer game going on while she was swimming.

hints.text: Notice that in the first table, six people say almost exactly the same sentence in Tariana, and the English translation is the same too. The only thing that changes is the last piece of the verb — and the only thing that changes in the story is HOW each person knows. Line those two columns up.

Tariana verbs are built as prefix + root + evidential suffix. The prefix tells you who the subject is (he, she, they, you), and the suffix tells you the speaker's source of information: seeing the event itself, hearing or smelling it, inferring it from physical traces left behind, assuming it from general knowledge, or being told about it by someone else. Each of the five sources has its own suffix.

Try the José table as practice. Antônia saw the game with her own eyes and says dimanikaka; Margarida only knew it was match day and says dimanikasika; Cândido found the equipment missing and says dimanikanihka. So the root is -manika- and the endings -ka, -sika, -nihka carry the three different kinds of knowledge. Compare dimanikaka with namanikaka to see what the prefix does.

explanationHtml:
What the puzzle is really about

In English, if you want to say how you know something, you add extra words: “I saw that he drank it”, “apparently he drank it”, “he must have drunk it”. In Tariana you cannot avoid saying it: every verb carries a little ending called an evidential, which marks your source of information. Leaving it out is like leaving out the past tense in English — the sentence is simply not grammatical.

That is why the first table has six people saying the same English sentence, He drank manioc-flour, in six slightly different ways.

Step 1: split the verb

Look at Antônia's and Margarida's sentences:

  • Diha kawhi-nuku diiɾaka
  • Diha kawhi-nuku diiɾamahka

Everything is identical up to diira-, then one has -ka and the other -mahka. Doing this across all six rows gives the verb shape di- + -ira- + evidential: a prefix meaning “he”, the root “drink”, and an ending.

Step 2: match each ending to a kind of evidence

EndingSource of informationExample evidence in the story
-kavisual: you saw the event happenAntônia saw Ismael drink it
-mahkanon-visual senses: you heard it, smelled itMargarida heard slurping; Emílio smelled it on his breath
-nihkainferred: you saw physical traces left behindCândido saw flour on the lip; the equipment was missing
-sikaassumed: general knowledge, habits, reasoningJoão knew Ismael took some every morning
-pidakareported: somebody told youIsmael told Maria; José's mum told Maria

The tricky pair is -mahka versus -nihka. Both are indirect, but -mahka is for perceiving the event as it happens with a sense other than sight, while -nihka is for working it out afterwards from what was left behind.

Step 3: the pronouns and prefixes

The second and third tables give us the person system:

diha / di-
he
duha / du-
she
naha / na-
they
piha / pi-
you

The free pronoun comes first in the sentence and the matching prefix sits on the verb: Naha iɾida namanikaka “they were playing soccer”. Personal names simply replace the pronoun, but the prefix stays: Óli dukwasika (Olívia, she-sleep-assumed), Leó dikwanihka (Leonardo, he-sleep-inferred).

Roots we can extract: -ira drink, -manika play, -ayha swim, -kwa sleep in a hammock, -ni make, -meyuta rake, -inu kill. Notice du- + -ayha gives duayha and pi- + -ayha gives piayha.

H1 and H2

(a) Cândido saw wet clothes — a trace, so inferred: duha duayhanihka. (b) Maria was told by Ismael's dad — reported: duha kawhi-nuku dunipidaka, built from João's dunimahka by swapping the ending.

For (c), the English is “You killed Ismael”, and the verb piinunihka already has the pi- “you” prefix, so the pronoun must be piha.

H3: reading the evidence backwards

Here the ending is given and you must decide which evidence fits. More than one option can fit, and some options fit no ending in the row.

  1. duayhaka is visual, so the speaker must have seen the swimming itself: B. A is general knowledge (-sika) and C is a trace (-nihka).
  2. dimeyutasika is assumed, so it has to come from a known habit: A. B is a smell (-mahka), C is a trace (-nihka).
  3. dimeyutamahka is non-visual sense. Both smelling him (A) and hearing him rake (B) count, so the answer is A and B. C is seeing the finished result, which is inference.
  4. dikwanihka is inferred from evidence. Seeing the slept-in hammock (B) and seeing that Leonardo looks well-rested (C) are both conclusions drawn from traces, so B and C. A is being told, which would need -pidaka.

H4: putting it all together

Each gap needs the right pronoun, the right prefix, the right root, and the right ending.

  • (d) “You were swimming”, overheard Olívia say so — that is a report: piha piayhapidaka.
  • (e) “He was raking the garden”, grass on his clothes is a trace: diha hinipuku dimeyutanihka.
  • (f) “Leonardo was sleeping in the hammock”, based on knowing his habits: leó dikwasika.
  • (g) “You drank manioc-flour”, a dirty cup is a trace: piha kawhi-nuku piiranihka.
  • (h) “They were playing soccer”, heard while swimming: naha iɾida namanikamahka.

One last detail worth noticing: the object kawhi “manioc-flour” carries the marker -nuku, which flags it as the topical object; iɾida “soccer” and hinipuku “garden” do not take it in this data, so just copy the pattern from the examples.
